title: Fiqh of Daily Prayers
description:
A detailed study of the jurisprudence (fiqh) of the five daily prayers, covering purification (Wudu and Ghusl), prayer times, the prayer itself, and common errors. This course presents the opinions of the four major Sunni schools of thought (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali) to provide a comprehensive understanding.

Prayer is the most important act of worship after the Shahada, and its correct performance is essential for every Muslim. This course goes beyond the basic requirements to explore the nuances and details that scholars have discussed for centuries.

Each lesson includes references from classical fiqh manuals and the opinions of the major scholars, helping the student understand the diversity of opinion within Sunni Islam while maintaining respect for all legitimate scholarly positions.
short_description: Master the jurisprudence of daily prayers with classical scholarly opinions and practical guidance.

modules.title: Purification: The Foundation of Prayer
modules.description: Understanding Wudu, Ghusl, and Tayammum as prerequisites for valid prayer.

lessons.title: The Importance and Ruling of Purification
lessons.content:
Purification (Taharah) is the foundation of prayer and a prerequisite for its validity. Without proper purification, no prayer is accepted. Allah (SWT) says: 'Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repenting and loves those who purify themselves.' (Quran 2:222)

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'No prayer is accepted without purification.' (Sahih Muslim 224). This hadith establishes that purification is a condition for the validity of prayer.

Purification in Islam is of two types:
1. Physical purification (Taharah) - removing najasah (impurity) from the body, clothes, and place of prayer.
2. Ritual purification (Hadath) - removing the state of hadath (ritual impurity) through Wudu, Ghusl, or Tayammum.

The scholars have identified several types of ritual purification:
1. Wudu (Ablution) - for minor hadath (minor ritual impurity)
2. Ghusl (Full body bath) - for major hadath (major ritual impurity)
3. Tayammum (Dry purification) - an alternative when water is unavailable or harmful
4. wiping over leather socks (Mash) - as a substitute for washing the feet

Imam al-Nawawi (رحمه الله) in Al-Majmu' explained that purification is not merely a physical act but a spiritual one. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When a Muslim performs Wudu and washes his face, every sin that he looked at with his eyes comes out from his face with the water. When he washes his hands, every sin they committed comes out from his hands with the water.' (Sahih Muslim 244)

lessons.title: Wudu: Conditions, Pillars, and Sunnah Acts
lessons.content:
Wudu (ablution) is the most common form of purification and is required for the validity of prayer. This lesson covers the conditions, pillars, obligatory acts, and sunnah acts of Wudu.

Conditions of Wudu (Shurut):
1. Being Muslim
2. Being of sound mind
3. Having reached the age of discernment
4. Intention (niyyah) - according to the majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali); the Hanafi school does not make intention a condition for validity but recommends it.
5. Using pure water (ma' Tahur)
6. Removing najasah from the areas washed
7. Time of Wudu - not performing Wudu during a time when it is prohibited (e.g., after Asr for Hanafis)

Pillars of Wudu (Arkan) - as mentioned in the Quran: 'O you who have believed, when you rise to [perform] prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows and wipe over your heads and [wash] your feet to the ankles.' (Quran 5:6)
1. Washing the entire face
2. Washing both arms including the elbows
3. Wiping the head (at least a quarter, according to the majority; one-quarter according to the Shafi'i school)
4. Washing both feet including the ankles

Sunnah acts of Wudu include:
- Saying Bismillah at the beginning
- Washing the hands three times before Wudu
- Using the Siwak (miswak)
- Rinsing the mouth and sniffing water into the nose
- Running fingers through the beard
- Wiping the ears
- Washing each limb three times
- Beginning with the right side
- Making du'a after Wudu

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever performs Wudu and does not mention the Name of Allah, his Wudu is not complete.' (Abu Dawud 101, graded Sahih). This hadith emphasizes the importance of Bismillah in Wudu.

The scholars differ on whether the Wudu breaks with touching private parts (without desire) or with laughing out loud during prayer. These differences are based on different interpretations of the hadith literature and are discussed in detail in the fiqh manuals.

lessons.title: Ghusl and Tayammum
lessons.content:
Ghusl (full body bath) is required after major ritual impurity, such as after sexual intercourse, ejaculation, menstruation, or postpartum bleeding. This lesson covers the requirements and method of Ghusl, as well as Tayammum as an alternative when water is unavailable.

Conditions for the validity of Ghusl:
1. Being Muslim, of sound mind, and having reached the age of discernment
2. Intention (niyyah) - to remove ritual impurity
3. Using pure water
4. Ensuring water reaches all parts of the body, including the hair

Pillars of Ghusl (according to the majority):
1. Intention (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i schools)
2. Rinsing the mouth
3. Sniffing water into the nose
4. Washing the entire body

The method of Ghusl:
1. Make the intention to perform Ghusl
2. Say Bismillah
3. Wash the hands three times
4. Cleanse the private parts
5. Perform Wudu (as for prayer)
6. Pour water over the head three times, ensuring it reaches the roots of the hair
7. Pour water over the right side of the body three times
8. Pour water over the left side of the body three times

Tayammum is an alternative to Wudu or Ghusl when water is unavailable, harmful, or insufficient. Allah (SWT) says: 'But if you are ill or on a journey or one of you comes from the place of relieving himself or you have contacted women and do not find water, then seek clean earth and wipe over your faces and hands [with it].' (Quran 4:43)

Conditions for Tayammum:
1. No water available, or water is harmful, or insufficient for purification
2. Using clean earth or sand
3. Striking the earth with both palms
4. Wiping the face and hands

The scholars differ on whether Tayammum can be made with dirt, stone, or other materials. The majority say it must be earth (turab), while some Hanafi scholars allow other materials. Tayammum invalidates with the same things that invalidate Wudu, except for sleep.

modules.title: Understanding Prayer Times
modules.description: The precise times for each of the five daily prayers according to classical scholarship.

lessons.title: The Beginning and End Times of Each Prayer
lessons.content:
Each of the five daily prayers has a specific time window during which it must be performed. Understanding these times is essential for the validity of the prayer.

1. Fajr (Dawn Prayer):
- Begins: When the true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq) appears - a white horizontal light in the eastern horizon
- Ends: At sunrise
- The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The time for Fajr is from the break of dawn until the sun has not yet risen.' (Sahih Muslim 612)
- The preferred time (waqt al-ikhtiyar) is from the appearance of true dawn until approximately 15-20 minutes before sunrise
- Praying at the very beginning of its time is from the Sunnah, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) consistently performed Fajr early

2. Dhuhr (Noon Prayer):
- Begins: When the sun passes its zenith (when the shadow of an object is at its shortest)
- Ends: When the shadow of an object equals its length (for the majority) or twice its length (for the Hanafi school)
- The preferred time is from approximately 15-20 minutes after the sun passes its zenith

3. Asr (Afternoon Prayer):
- Begins: When the shadow of an object equals its length (according to the majority) or twice its length (Hanafi school)
- Ends: At sunset
- The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever catches one rak'ah of Asr before the sun sets has caught Asr.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 579)

4. Maghrib (Sunset Prayer):
- Begins: At sunset
- Ends: When the twilight (shafaq) disappears completely
- The preferred time is from sunset until approximately 15-20 minutes after sunset

5. Isha (Night Prayer):
- Begins: When the twilight disappears completely
- Ends: At midnight (according to the majority) or until the break of dawn (according to the Hanafi school)
- The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The time for Isha prayer is until midnight.' (Sahih Muslim 612)

The scholars have also discussed the concept of 'Ihtiyat' (precautionary prayer time), which is the extended time beyond the preferred time. Praying during this time is valid but not preferred. The only prayer that should not be delayed is Fajr, as praying it at sunrise is considered prohibited by many scholars.

lessons.title: Combining and Delaying Prayers
lessons.content:
The scholars have discussed the conditions under which combining or delaying prayers is permissible. Understanding these rulings is important for travelers, those with valid excuses, and others.

Combining Prayers (Jam' al-Salatayn):
1. During Hajj: Combining Dhuhr with Asr at 'Arafah, and Maghrib with Isha at Muzdalifah. This is based on the Sunnah of the Prophet (peace be upon him) during Hajj.
2. For travelers: The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) permit combining prayers during travel. The Hanafi school does not permit combining except in cases of rain, illness, or other valid excuses.
3. For the sick: If a person is unable to pray at the proper time due to illness, they may combine prayers.
4. During rain: Many scholars permit combining during heavy rain or when the ground is muddy.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) combined Maghrib and Isha at 'Arafah and Muzdalifah during Hajj, but did not combine during normal travel. However, he permitted combining when there was hardship.

Delaying Prayers (Takhlif al-Salatayn):
1. The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) permit delaying prayers for a valid reason, such as travel or illness, as long as the prayer is performed before its time expires.
2. The Hanafi school is more restrictive, requiring that each prayer be performed at its proper time except in cases of extreme hardship.
3. The Prophet (peace be upon him) delayed the prayer of the people of Khaibar until night, which is mentioned in the hadith of Jabir (Sahih al-Bukhari 4011).

Combining without a valid reason is considered disliked (makruh) by the majority and prohibited by the Hanafi school. The scholars emphasize that combining or delaying should only be done when there is a genuine need, as it is a relaxation of the general rule of praying each prayer at its proper time.

The concept of 'Qada' (making up missed prayers) is also important. If a person misses a prayer due to sleep, forgetfulness, or other valid reasons, they should make it up as soon as they remember. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever oversleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers, for there is no expiation for it other than that.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 597, Sahih Muslim 477)

modules.title: The Prayer Itself: Rak'ahs and Actions
modules.description: The detailed steps of performing the prayer, including the Takbir, recitation, bowing, prostration, and tashahhud.

lessons.title: The Opening of the Prayer and Recitation
lessons.content:
The prayer begins with the Takbir al-Ihram (saying 'Allahu Akbar' - Allah is the Greatest) and includes the recitation of Surah Al-Fatihah and other verses from the Quran.

1. Takbir al-Ihram: This is the opening of the prayer and marks the transition from the state of not praying to the state of praying. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The key to prayer is purification (Wudu), its beginning is the Takbir, and its end is the Taslim.' (Sunan an-Nasa'i 118, graded Sahih)

2. Qiyam (Standing): The worshipper stands facing the Qiblah, with hands raised to the level of the shoulders or chest, according to the majority. The Hanafi school raises the hands to the level of the earlobes. The hands are then folded below the navel (Hanafi) or on the chest (Shafi'i, Hanbali, Maliki).

3. Recitation of Surah Al-Fatihah: This is a pillar of the prayer. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Quran (Al-Fatihah), his prayer is incomplete.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 756). Al-Fatihah is recited in every rak'ah.

4. Recitation after Al-Fatihah: In the first two rak'ahs of the Fard (obligatory) prayer, additional Quranic verses are recited after Al-Fatihah. In the remaining rak'ahs, only Al-Fatihah is recited (according to the majority). The Hanafi school recites in the third and fourth rak'ahs as well.

5. Saying 'Ameen': After Al-Fatihah, the worshipper says 'Ameen' (O Allah, respond). The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When the Imam says 'Ameen', say 'Ameen', for the one whose 'Ameen' coincides with the 'Ameen' of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 780)

6. Reciting additional verses: After Al-Fatihah and saying Ameen, the worshipper recites a short surah or verses from the Quran. The scholars recommend reciting different surahs in the first and second rak'ahs.

The scholars differ on the number of verses to recite and the minimum amount required for the recitation to be valid. The majority agree that at least three short verses or one long verse is sufficient for the first rak'ah, while the second rak'ah requires less.

lessons.title: Ruku', Sujud, and the Tashahhud
lessons.content:
These are the essential movements and positions of the prayer, each carrying specific rulings and spiritual significance.

1. Ruku' (Bowing): After completing the recitation, the worshipper says 'Allahu Akbar' and bows, placing the hands on the knees, keeping the back straight, and looking down. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you bows, let him not raise his head until his bones settle in their places, and do not lower your head for yourselves.' (Ahmad, graded Sahih). While bowing, the worshipper says: 'Subhana Rabbiyal 'Adheem' (Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great) at least three times.

2. Rising from Ruku' (I'tidal): After bowing, the worshipper rises to a standing position, saying: 'Sami'allahu liman hamidah' (Allah hears those who praise Him), and then: 'Rabbana walakal hamd' (Our Lord, and to You be praise). The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The one who says after Ruku': 'Sami'allahu liman hamidah, Rabbana walakal hamd' will have his sins forgiven.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 796)

3. Sujud (Prostration): The worshipper goes down to the ground, placing the forehead, nose, palms, knees, and toes on the ground. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you prostrates, let him place his knees on the ground first, then his hands, and then his forehead.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 828). While prostrating, the worshipper says: 'Subhana Rabbiyal A'la' (Glory be to my Lord, the Most High) at least three times.

4. Sitting between Prostrations (Jalsa): After the first prostration, the worshipper sits upright, saying: 'Allahummaghfirli warhamni wajburni wahdini warzuqni' (O Allah, forgive me, have mercy on me, strengthen me, guide me, and provide for me). This is mentioned in the hadith of Mu'adh (Sahih Muslim 399).

5. Second Sujud: The worshipper performs a second prostration identical to the first.

6. Tashahhud: After completing the second rak'ah (or the last rak'ah), the worshipper sits for the Tashahhud. The hands are placed on the thighs, near the knees, with the index finger raised during the declaration of faith. The Tashahhud includes: 'At-Tahiyyat lillahi was-salawatu wat-tayyibat, as-salamu 'alayka ayyuhan-Nabiyyu wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh, as-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibadillahis-salihin. Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah wahdahu la sharika lahu, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan 'abduhu wa rasuluh.'

The scholars differ on several details, such as whether the index finger should be raised or moved, whether the worshipper should say 'Rabbighfir li warhamni' during sitting, and the exact wording of the Tashahhud. These differences are based on different interpretations of the hadith literature and are all acceptable within Sunni Islam.

lessons.title: Taslim and Sunnah Prayers
lessons.content:
The prayer concludes with the Taslim (saying 'As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah' twice), turning the head to the right and left. This lesson also covers the Sunnah prayers that accompany the obligatory prayers.

1. Taslim: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The key to prayer is purification, its beginning is the Takbir, and its end is the Taslim.' (Sunan an-Nasa'i 118). The worshipper turns the head to the right, saying 'As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah,' and then to the left, saying the same.

2. Sunnah al-Mu'akkadah (Emphasized Sunnah Prayers): These are prayers that the Prophet (peace be upon him) consistently performed and are strongly recommended:
- Two rak'ahs before Fajr
- Four rak'ahs before Dhuhr and two after
- Two rak'ahs after Maghrib
- Two rak'ahs after Isha
- Witr prayer (three rak'ahs) after Isha

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever prays twelve rak'ahs of Sunnah prayer, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise: four before Dhuhr, two after it, two after Maghrib, two after Isha, and two before Fajr.' (Sahih Muslim 728)

3. Sunnah Ghair Mu'akkadah (Non-emphasized Sunnah): These are prayers that the Prophet sometimes performed and sometimes omitted. Examples include two rak'ahs before Asr and two rak'ahs before Maghrib.

4. Witr Prayer: This is a prayer performed after Isha and before Fajr. The minimum is one rak'ah, the maximum is eleven, and the preferred is three. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The night prayer (Witr) is one rak'ah after eleven rak'ahs.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1100)

5. Rawatib (Supplementary) Prayers: These are voluntary prayers performed before or after the obligatory prayers. They have different levels of recommendation, from the most emphasized (Mu'akkadah) to the least.

The scholars emphasize the importance of maintaining the Sunnah prayers, as they increase a Muslim's reward, compensate for any deficiencies in the obligatory prayer, and serve as a means of drawing closer to Allah (SWT).

modules.title: Common Prayer Errors and Their Corrections
modules.description: Addressing frequent mistakes in prayer with scholarly solutions and authentic references.

lessons.title: Errors in Purification and Prayer Times
lessons.content:
Many Muslims make errors in purification and observing prayer times that can affect the validity of their prayer. This lesson addresses the most common errors and their corrections.

Errors in Wudu:
1. Not washing the elbows completely - The Quran specifies 'to the elbows' (Quran 5:6). Many people wash only the forearm and leave the elbow dry.
2. Not wiping the entire head - The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) require wiping at least a quarter of the head. The Shafi'i school requires wiping the entire head.
3. Not washing the feet properly - The Prophet (peace be upon him) warned about the punishment of the feet in Hellfire: 'Woe to the heels from the Fire.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 165). This emphasizes the importance of washing the heels completely.
4. Not performing Wudu in the correct order - The scholars recommend performing the acts of Wudu in the order mentioned in the Quran.

Errors in Prayer Times:
1. Praying Fajr at sunrise - The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever catches the Fajr prayer is like one who has taken the night in worship.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 574). This indicates the importance of catching Fajr before sunrise.
2. Delaying Dhuhr until Asr time - This is a common error, especially among those who work. Dhuhr should be prayed in its preferred time, approximately 15-20 minutes after the sun passes its zenith.
3. Praying Maghrib immediately at sunset - While praying early is permissible, it is Sunnah to delay Maghrib slightly. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to delay Maghrib a little.
4. Delaying Isha until midnight - The preferred time for Isha is when the twilight disappears, which is earlier than midnight.

The scholars emphasize that while these errors do not necessarily invalidate the prayer (unless they are severe), they reduce its reward and are contrary to the Sunnah. Muslims should strive to pray each prayer at its proper time and perform purification correctly.

lessons.title: Errors in Prayer Actions and Recitation
lessons.content:
This lesson addresses common errors in the actions and recitation during prayer, with scholarly solutions and authentic references.

Errors in Actions:
1. Raising hands during the prayer - Many people raise their hands at times other than the Takbir al-Ihram and when going down for Ruku'. The Prophet (peace be upon him) raised his hands only at the beginning of the prayer and when going down for Ruku'.
2. Saying 'Ameen' out loud - The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) say that the 'Ameen' should be said silently. The Hanafi school says it should be said aloud. The scholars differ on which is better.
3. Not completing the Ruku' and Sujud - The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The worst of thieves is the one who steals from his prayer.' When asked how he steals from his prayer, he said: 'By not completing its Ruku' and Sujud.' (Ahmad, graded Sahih). This hadith emphasizes the importance of completing each position.
4. Moving or fidgeting during prayer - This can invalidate the prayer according to some scholars, especially if it is excessive.
5. Placing the hands on the hips during Sujud - This is not from the Sunnah and is considered disliked by the scholars.

Errors in Recitation:
1. Reciting Al-Fatihah incorrectly - The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When you pray, say: Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil 'alamin. This is Umm al-Quran and Umm al-Kitab, and it is a sevenfold recitation that is repeated in what Allah has revealed.' (Sahih Muslim 808)
2. Reciting too quickly - The scholars recommend reciting with tarteel (measured recitation) and contemplating the meaning of the verses.
3. Not reciting Al-Fatihah in the third and fourth rak'ahs - The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) say that Al-Fatihah must be recited in every rak'ah. The Hanafi school says it is not required in the third and fourth rak'ahs.
4. Reciting very long surahs - While permissible, this can be burdensome for the congregation. The scholars recommend reciting moderately.

The scholars emphasize that the prayer is a comprehensive act of worship that requires focus, humility, and proper execution. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you prays, let him have complete wudu, and let him face the Qiblah, and let him say Allahu Akbar, then let him recite what is easy for him from the Quran.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 757)

lessons.title: Errors in Tashahhud and Taslim
lessons.content:
The Tashahhud and Taslim are essential parts of the prayer that many Muslims recite incorrectly. This lesson covers the most common errors and their corrections.

Errors in Tashahhud:
1. Reciting too quickly - The Tashahhud should be recited slowly and with deliberation. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you sits in the prayer, let him say: At-Tahiyyat lillahi...' and then mentioned the complete Tashahhud.
2. Not raising the index finger - The scholars differ on when and how the index finger should be raised. The majority (Hanbali, some Shafi'i) say it should be raised when saying 'La ilaha' and folded when saying 'illallah'. The Hanafi school says it should be raised throughout the Tashahhud. The Maliki school says it should be raised at 'La ilaha' and lowered at 'illallah'.
3. Making du'a (supplication) during the Tashahhud - While permissible, many people make long supplications during the Tashahhud, which can be burdensome for the Imam and congregation.
4. Not completing the Tashahhud - The Tashahhud must be recited in full, including the Salawat upon the Prophet (peace be upon him).

Errors in Taslim:
1. Not turning the head fully to the right and left - The scholars say that the head should be turned to the point that the cheek is visible to the person sitting next to you.
2. Saying Taslim too quickly - The Taslim should be said slowly and with deliberation. The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to say: 'As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah' and then 'As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah' with a pause in between.
3. Making du'a after Taslim - While it is Sunnah to make du'a after the Taslim, many people make it part of the prayer itself. The scholars say that the prayer ends with the Taslim, and any du'a after that is voluntary.
4. Turning the head to the left before the right - The Sunnah is to turn the head to the right first, then to the left.

The scholars emphasize that the Tashahhud is a right of Allah and a right of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and it should be recited with care and respect. The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught his companions the Tashahhud directly and encouraged them to recite it properly.

These errors, while they may not invalidate the prayer according to the majority, reduce its reward and are contrary to the Sunnah. Muslims should strive to correct these errors and improve the quality of their prayer.

modules.title: Praying in Congregation
modules.description: The rulings and etiquette of praying in congregation (Jama'ah) in the mosque.

lessons.title: The Virtue and Ruling of Congregational Prayer
lessons.content:
Praying in congregation (Salat al-Jama'ah) is one of the most important acts of communal worship in Islam. It is strongly recommended (Sunnah Mu'akkadah) for men and is held in the mosque.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The prayer in congregation is better than the prayer alone by twenty-seven degrees.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 645, Sahind Muslim 650). This hadith emphasizes the immense reward of praying in congregation.

The scholars differ on whether congregational prayer is obligatory (fard) or Sunnah Mu'akkadah:
- The Hanbali school says it is fard kifayah (communal obligation) - if some people pray in congregation, the obligation is lifted from the rest.
- The Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanafi schools say it is Sunnah Mu'akkadah (strongly recommended).

The mosque (masjid) is the designated place for congregational prayer. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The best of places is the mosque, and the worst of places is the market.' (Sunan Ibn Majah 733, graded Sahih)

The Imam leads the congregation and is responsible for the correctness of the prayer. The scholars specify conditions for the Imam:
1. He must be Muslim, male, and of sound mind.
2. He should have knowledge of the prayer and Quran recitation.
3. He should be of good character and appearance.
4. He should not lead while there is someone more qualified present (according to some scholars).

The Ma'mum (follower) should follow the Imam carefully and should not start the prayer before the Imam unless the Imam is late. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you comes to the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs of greeting the mosque (Tahiyyat al-Masjid) before sitting.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 429)

lessons.title: Praying Behind the Imam and Rows
lessons.content:
The proper arrangement of rows (sufuf) and following the Imam are essential aspects of congregational prayer that many Muslims overlook.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Straighten your rows and stand close together, for indeed I see you from behind my back.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 717). This hadith emphasizes the importance of straight and close rows.

Conditions of the Rows:
1. The rows should be straight and aligned with the Qiblah.
2. There should be no gaps between the worshippers.
3. Each person should stand shoulder to shoulder with the person next to them.
4. The front rows should be filled first.
5. Women should pray behind the men.

Following the Imam:
1. The Ma'mum should follow the Imam's movements exactly.
2. The Ma'mum should not say 'Ameen' out loud (according to the majority) until the Imam has finished saying it.
3. The Ma'mum should not recite Al-Fatihah or additional Quran while the Imam is reciting.
4. The Ma'mum should go into Ruku' after the Imam, not before.
5. The Ma'mum should say 'Sami'allahu liman hamidah' when the Imam rises from Ruku'.
6. The Ma'mum should say 'Rabbana walakal hamd' when the Imam is fully upright.
7. The Ma'mum should say 'Ameen' silently after Al-Fatihah (according to the majority).

Errors in following the Imam:
1. Starting the prayer before the Imam - This is not permissible. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Imam is to be followed, so when he says Allahu Akbar, say Allahu Akbar, and when he says Sami'allahu liman hamidah, say Rabbana walakal hamd.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 722)
2. Saying Allahu Akbar before the Imam - This is also not permissible.
3. Reciting during the Imam's recitation - The Ma'mum should remain silent while the Imam is reciting.
4. Moving before the Imam - The Ma'mum should wait for the Imam to complete each movement before following.

The scholars emphasize that congregational prayer is an act of unity and discipline. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever hears the call (Adhan) and does not come to the mosque, his prayer is not accepted.' (Sunan an-Nasa'i 670). This hadith emphasizes the importance of responding to the Adhan and attending the mosque for congregational prayer.
